articles.title: Global Web Encryption Shaken by Eight Illicit TLS Certificates
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet. As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices. One word: bonkers The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here – Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide. “This will be a massive cleanup job, bigger than Heartbleed,” Filippo Valsorda, a cryptography engineer and a cryptography maintainer for the open source Go programming language, told Ars. “There will be a very, very long tail, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, unmaintained CLI tools that shipped their own copy of the roots (which is common in some ecosystems, like Python). Also, Linux distributions are still rolling out updates, some of them are not ready yet, and then system administrators will need to apply them to a lot of machines.” Heartbleed is the name of a critical vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptography library. In 2014, it came under mass exploitation . Exploits let many unaffiliated hackers decrypt TLS-protected exchanges between parties. They also recovered private TLS certificate keys, session cookies, and passwords. The attacks compromised thousands of servers, some belonging to large companies and government agencies around the world. Recovery required a long series of steps that took years. Steps included patching OpenSSL on all affected devices, reissuing millions of TLS keys, revoking old certificates, rotating passwords and session tokens and updating embedded devices and other forgotten systems—something that was extremely time- and resource-intensive, especially at Internet scale. “Every time you need a lot of different people in different contexts to do something, it will take a long time,” Valsorda explained. “This time it’s worse because there’s more contexts, more people, and more heterogeneity.” The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2 384 , or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237. “That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???” Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.” At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place. As noted, most browsers have already blocked the intermediate certificates. The exception appears to be Edge running on Windows 10, which at the time this article went live was still connecting to 12 vulnerable hosts. In response to questions asking why and if the company has plans to do so, a Microsoft representative the company will be in touch if it has anything to “share.” Meanwhile, Signal, WhatsApp, Wireguard, and other apps that don’t rely on TLS for confidentiality aren’t affected. This page and the emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com site show apps known to be patched so far. The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions. One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network—at a coffee shop, university, or other organization—face much less of a challenge. Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. Contact him on Signal at DanArs.82. 55 Comments

articles.title: Dutch Intelligence Backlash Over US Direct Server Seizure Demands
articles.content: ‘Zullen we nog een beetje lawaai maken?”, roept Sanne Stevens. Kartonnen bordjes gaan omhoog, het getoeter van een vuvuzela zwelt aan, Stevens zelf schreeuwt: „Geen collaboratie met fascisme, geen collaboratie met Trump!” Het geluid weerkaatst tussen de torens van het Amsterdamse Openbaar Ministerie aan het IJ, stratenmakers kijken op. Toch is de opkomst gering: zo’n vijftien demonstranten komen deze dinsdag in het geweer tegen het overdragen van de inhoud van een server aan de Verenigde Staten. Die server is van de Italiaanse internetdienstverlener Autistici/Inventati (A/I) en stond in Amsterdam. Op basis van een Amerikaans rechtshulpverzoek nam de Amsterdamse politie de server vorige week in beslag, om een kopie te maken van de inhoud en die door te sturen naar de VS. Dat laatste is nog niet is gebeurd. Wat er gebeurt als de Amerikaanse regering tegen je is, voelen in Nederland aanklagers en rechters van het Internationaal Strafhof al, tegen wie de regering-Trump vergaande sancties heeft opgelegd. Met de actie tegen het Italiaanse internetcollectief ervaren ook activistische groeperingen en individuen, van wie blogs gehost werden door A/I, de gevolgen. Neem Sanne Stevens, organisator van het protest dinsdag: het Justice, Equity and Technology Project van de London School of Economics, waaraan zij verbonden is, had zijn site ondergebracht bij het platform. „Ik had een A/I-mailadres.” De onlangs opgeheven organisatie werd gerund door vrijwilligers en bood gratis e-mailadressen en hosting van websites aan. Daar maakten wereldwijd zo’n twintigduizend mensen en organisaties gebruik van. A/I begon een kwart eeuw geleden als hackerscollectief, maar vormde zich om tot een in Italië geregistreerde organisatie zonder winstoogmerk, gerund door vrijwilligers en gefinancierd met donaties. A/I was volgens de eigen omschrijving ‘antikapitalistisch’. Ze wilden niet verdienen aan de data van hun ‘cliënten’ en vonden online privacy belangrijk. De organisaties die bij A/I een website hadden, waren in de praktijk ook vaak antikapitalistisch en noemden zich geregeld ‘antifascistisch’ of kortweg ‘antifa’. De Amerikaanse regering beschouwt ‘antifa’ tegenwoordig als een terreurbeweging. Op 26 augustus werd A/I dan ook toegevoegd aan de Amerikaanse sanctielijst, omdat het de digitale infrastructuur zou leveren voor gewelddadige antifa-cellen en andere links-extremistische militanten wereldwijd. Voor het offline halen van websites die geweld of andere illegale zaken promoten, en bijvoorbeeld beelden van kindermisbruik verspreiden, bestaan procedures. Die zijn in het geval van de websites die op de servers van A/I draaiden niet gevolgd. Het gebruik van een terreursanctie om een internetdienstverlener in Europa uit de lucht te halen is grof geschut, dat direct gevolgen had. De organisatie verloor binnen een dag zijn PayPal-account, dat werd gebruikt voor donaties en de .org-domeinnaam. Vervolgens bevroor de Italiaanse bank waar A/I een rekening had de toegang daartoe. Al snel besloten de vrijwilligers dat ze hun energie beter konden steken in het opheffen van hun organisatie. De afwikkeling daarvan is in volle gang. Bij het kleinschalige protest in Amsterdam wordt een spandoek ontrold. „We are all A/I”, staat erop. Bert Prins (35) uit Den Haag leunt op een dranghek bij de stratenmakers. „Door het opsturen van de serverinhoud, voelt het alsof de VS Nederland hebben gekoloniseerd. We zijn afhankelijk gemaakt van Amerikaanse tech. Ik ben zelf al tien jaar van alle sociale media af, maar ik noem mezelf dan ook een privacywappie.” Sanne Stevens komt bij hem staan. Stevens: „Misschien zijn mensen lamgeslagen door hoe snel de ontwikkelingen in de VS gaan, terwijl het zo zorgelijk is hoe het OM zich voor het karretje van Trump laat spannen.” Aan de hand van wat A/I overkwam is goed te zien hoe groot de macht van de VS is in de digitale wereld en de financiële sector. De zaak word niet alleen gevolgd door de demonstranten in Amsterdam, maar ook door techbedrijven, organisaties die zich met online burgerrechten bezighouden en Tweede Kamerleden. Afgelopen weken stelden regeringspartij D66 en de oppositiepartijen Pro, SP en de Partij voor de Dieren Kamervragen, waarin ze nadrukkelijk ook de koppeling maken met de sancties tegen het Internationaal Strafhof. Het was een Amerikaans rechtshulpverzoek waardoor het OM de politie opdracht gaf de server van A/I in Amsterdam in beslag te nemen. Omdat Nederland en de VS juridisch samenwerken op basis van een rechtsbijstandsverdrag, waren er geen gronden om medewerking aan dat rechtshulpverzoek te weigeren, verklaarde het OM. „Het rechtshulpverzoek gaat over een strafbaar feit dat in Nederland ook zou worden vervolgd.” Na een uurtje ‘lawaai maken’ bergen de demonstranten hun bordjes op. Iemand oppert, half grappend: „Kunnen we die server niet gewoon gaan ophalen?” Maak NRC jouw voorkeursbron op Google Bij Google kan je nu zelf aangeven welke nieuwsbronnen jij vaker wil zien in je zoekresultaten. articles.title: TP-Link Promises American Router Manufacturing to Avert Trump Tariffs
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav TP-Link yesterday announced plans to assemble Wi-Fi routers in the US, as the company attempts to get the Trump administration’s approval to sell its newest routers to American consumers. The timing is uncertain, as TP-Link’s press release said it expects US-based assembly to begin “as early as” 2027. TP-Link’s application to sell new routers in the US could be rejected by the Trump administration or remain pending long enough to push the US-based assembly to 2028. “Pending US regulatory approval, TP-Link expects domestic assembly of its groundbreaking Wi-Fi 8 home networking product line to begin as early as next year,” the company said. TP-Link said it signed a Letter of Intent with US company Keytronic, which agreed “to become a primary domestic manufacturing partner for TP-Link, supporting assembly of the company’s advanced networking portfolio in Corinth, Mississippi.” TP-Link can’t sell its Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US because of the Federal Communications Commission ban on consumer-grade routers produced wholly or partly in other countries. Previous TP-Link routers that were already approved for import and sale are still available. What counts as a US router is unclear The FCC has given exemptions to a number of prominent router makers, but TP-Link’s history as a Chinese company is making it difficult to obtain FCC clearance. Founded in China in 1996, TP-Link moved its headquarters to California in October 2024. It says that “TP-Link Systems devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam and TP-Link Systems is an independent, US company that is not owned or controlled by any foreign government.” While TP-Link assembles routers in Vietnam, most of the components are reportedly imported from China. TP-Link’s plan to assemble routers in the US will still require it to import components, but the company hopes investment in the US will help it gain the Trump administration’s favor. While the FCC is urging router makers to move more of their operations to the US, a TP-Link official said the government has provided no clear guidance on how much US manufacturing is enough to obtain an exemption from the foreign router ban. “There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag . Kovsky said that many components “are just not available from a domestic source, and this is not a TP-Link issue. This is an issue for all manufacturers that are trying to onshore manufacturing.” In a letter to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr and the agency’s commissioners last week, Kovsky said TP-Link is proposing “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs.” TP-Link struggles to convince Trump admin TP-Link’s letter said it will make the proposed investment if it receives approval to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US. “This investment would build upon TP-Link’s existing US footprint, which includes a global headquarters in Irvine, Calif., and more than 700 US employees,” TP-Link told the FCC. “As part of this investment, TP-Link would begin assembling these Wi-Fi 8 devices in the United States by next year, and the devices will incorporate software and firmware developed, written, and stored in the United States by TP-Link’s US engineering organization.” The FCC isn’t the only agency that TP-Link has to convince. The FCC process for issuing exemptions from the ban requires each router maker to first obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its devices do not pose national security risks. Router makers that received exemptions so far include Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Amazon and its Eero subsidiary, Calix, Nokia, SpaceX’s Starlink division, and others. TP-Link urged the Trump administration to ensure that its “reviewers fairly apply the same consistent review standards to TP-Link as have been applied to all other applicants.” TP-Link’s 2024 move to the US came amid investigations into high-profile attacks linked to the Chinese government, including a botnet composed mostly of TP-Link routers. The Russian GRU also compromised TP-Link routers to steal information, US intelligence agencies said in April 2026 . TP-Link is far from the only router maker with security problems. For example, so-called AirSnitch attacks described in research this year were reported to work on routers made by Netgear, D-Link, Ubiquiti, Cisco, and those running DD-WRT and OpenWrt. Republican AGs urge FCC to stand firm TP-Link’s letter to the FCC last week said its application for an exemption provides “complete responses” to questions about its corporate structure and manufacturing and supply chain. “TP-Link prioritizes the security of US consumer networking data; user data processed by TP-Link’s US products is encrypted and housed on Amazon Web Services infrastructure in Virginia,” the company said. “And of course, TP-Link does not, and will not, share customer network data with foreign governments or unauthorized third parties.” TP-Link also faces opposition from Republican state attorneys general. The AGs from Florida, Montana, Iowa, and Nebraska sued TP-Link this month , alleging that it lied to consumers about its connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs then sent a letter to the FCC questioning TP-Link’s claims regarding router security and the company’s independence from China. The letter urged the FCC to require remedies for “past and ongoing state-law violations” in its review of TP-Link’s application and to protect router users “from exploitation by the Chinese Communist Party.” Jon Brodkin Senior IT Reporter Jon Brodkin Senior IT Reporter 30 Comments

articles.title: ConnectWise Supply Chain Infiltration Triggered by Exposed API Credential
articles.content: A portion of ConnectWise’s customers have been adrift for days, and hundreds are compromised, as the company’s efforts to restore its Cloud Backup service remain underway with no confirmed timeline for when customers can regain access. The company temporarily shut down multiple services Saturday after a threat actor gained access to a highly sensitive credential that allowed its customers to connect the vendor’s application with Microsoft 365 environments.  The threat actor, which hasn’t been identified, used the application programming interface (API) secret to compromise a series of ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers’ Microsoft 365 applications, including Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Cloud Backup, MS Graph and Partner Center, according to Huntress. Researchers observed an initial wave of attacks Friday, and by late Saturday Huntress “had seen sign-in activity from the malicious infrastructure across almost 1,000 Entra tenants, with more than 300 of those sign-ins appearing to succeed,” Jonathan Semon, principal security operations analyst at Huntress, told CyberScoop. The cybersecurity company, which primarily supports small- to mid-sized businesses, confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants and said additional compromises beyond its telemetry are likely.  ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security and Cloud Management services about two days after researchers observed an initial wave of unauthorized sign-ins.  “ConnectWise is continuing its investigation and remediation following unauthorized access to application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick,” a company spokesperson wrote in an email. “We are monitoring our entire environment around the clock,” the company said in a security advisory . “Since mitigations began on October 17 at 05:00 UTC, we have not observed successful threat activity in the environments we monitor. This does not establish whether individual partner or customer Microsoft 365 tenants were affected; each potentially affected tenant still requires review.” Microsoft Threat Intelligence said it observed broad successful sign-ins from a malicious IP address on Oct. 15. “Follow-on activity included Microsoft Graph API reconnaissance and attempts to add additional credentials on the related service principal in target tenants to maintain direct access as a backdoor,” the company said in a LinkedIn post .  The root cause of the breach and ensuing fallout remains under investigation, and the company declined to answer questions about how attackers obtained the credential for ConnectWise Cloud Backup. Researchers at Huntress and Todyl, which conducted its own investigation, characterized the secret and its chain of command as critical. “Because it’s a multi-tenant application, anyone holding that credential can request access tokens in any tenant where the application is installed, without any action by the customer,” Semon said. Sign-ins, which were performed by an automated tool, also gave the attacker the technical ability to read and write mail and files across various Microsoft 365 applications, Todyl wrote in a blog post .  Highly privileged access granted by the credential for ConnectWise Cloud Backup allowed attackers to bypass security controls, including multi-factor authentication, and establish additional access. “In the tenants where we saw post-compromise activity, the account associated with the application elevated its own privileges and added new credentials to other applications in the tenant. That would let someone keep access even after the original application was disabled,” Semon said. ConnectWise and researchers haven’t attributed the attacks to any known threat actors and none have publicly claimed responsibility. The company said restoration efforts remain underway, but it hasn’t provided a timeline for when customers can regain access. ConnectWise and researchers shared indicators of compromise to help potentially exposed customers hunt for malicious activity in their systems. Yet, the vendor and third-party companies responding to confirmed attacks, encouraged customers to disable any affected applications even if they don’t see anything unusual in their logs.

articles.title: Quantum Error Correction Transcends Breakeven Threshold in Historic Advance
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Running complicated algorithms on quantum computing hardware is going to require the use of logical qubits, where collections of hardware qubits are linked together in ways that allow errors to be detected and corrected. In general, the more hardware qubits you dedicate to each logical qubit, the better the chances are of identifying errors. But, given that the hardware qubits are prone to errors, adding more of them also increases the probability that errors will occur. If the hardware error rate is too high, then growing the logical qubit will only make matters worse. Fortunately, several companies have demonstrated hardware where the error rate is not too high. Several demonstrations show logical qubits are beyond the breakeven point, where adding more qubits improves performance. The problem is that the improvement isn’t very dramatic. To lower error rates to levels we’ll need to run complex algorithms, we’d have to add a completely impractical number of qubits to each logical qubit. On Monday, Quantinuum announced that its current generation of hardware is capable of scaling well beyond the breakeven point. Each step up in the size of logical qubits improved some measures of their performance by a factor of over 10. Error correction codes and scaling To understand the results, we must take a little detour through the ideas behind error correction. A logical qubit consists of a set of qubits that hold data, and another set that is used for measurements, all of them entangled to others. There are various error correction “codes,” each of which has a different geometry of entangled connections among its constituent qubits. During operations, measurements of the appropriate qubits produce what’s called “syndrome data,” which can be interpreted to provide an indication of whether an error has occurred within the logical qubit, as well as where and its nature. Depending on their geometry, error codes have a number of key properties: how many hardware qubits are needed for it to work, how many individual logical qubits it hosts, and something called the distance, which is a rough measure of how many errors can occur simultaneously before the logical qubit fails. Members of some families of error correction codes differ in a fairly simple way: Each step up in size (which may require multiple hardware qubits) means a greater distance. So by adding more hardware qubits, you can create a similar geometry while providing a greater distance. These sorts of codes can be used to measure how well a given quantum processor’s error correction scales. You start by measuring the error rate of the logical qubit with a small distance, say three. Then you can devote more hardware qubits to the text and measure it at a distance of five, repeat the process for a distance of seven, and so on until you run out of hardware qubits to add. If the hardware is past the breakeven point, then the error rate will be lower with each step up in distance. And the scaling factor—how much better the error rate gets at each step—gives you a sense of how far beyond breakeven it is. This matters a great deal for practical reasons. If each step up in size cuts the error rate by a factor of 10, then you only have to step up in distance a few times to get the error rate down by a considerable amount. If, by contrast, the scaling factor is closer to two, then you have to go up in distance many, many times to get the same effect. So far, most demonstrations of scaling beyond the breakeven point have seen the error rate drop by something much closer to two than 10. Which may mean that we’d need to add many thousands of hardware qubits to the logical qubit just to get the error rate down to what we’d need to run a complex algorithm. Meet Helios Quantinuum builds what are called trapped ion quantum computers. As their name implies, each qubit is stored in an ion, an atom that has lost one or more of its electrons. Because they are charged, it’s possible to manipulate these using electrical fields generated by electronics, moving them around and rearranging them. The company’s latest hardware , called Helios, rotates the ions around a ring, selectively shifting the appropriate ones into one of two arms where measurements and operations of the ions’ quantum states can be performed using lasers. Because any two ions can be brought into these arms at the same time, it’s possible to entangle any ion with any other, providing Helios the ability to host essentially any error code. In general, the company’s hardware has relatively low error rates. But previous iterations didn’t have enough qubits to increase the distance of logical qubits very much. But with Helios, the company finally had the ability to use versions of an error correction code (called a color code) with distances of three, five, and seven (though it only has enough hardware qubits to host a single distance of seven logical qubits at a time). In addition, Quantinuum has made a key change in how its processor operates. A significant number of errors in earlier Quantinuum processors occurred through what’s called “leakage.” This occurs when a qubit, instead of occupying one of the two energy states used for calculations, ends up in a nearby energy state that’s not normally used. Now, the company is using a scheme that uses laser light to selectively manipulate those qubits that have leaked into other energy states and bring them back to one of the two used for computation. This suppresses leakage errors by a factor of 6.5 and can be done at the same time the system is using lasers to cool the ions. It has also developed a software-based system that can take any leaked data-holding qubits and swap them out for measurement qubits, which can then be reset and reused. Color coding For one of the two experiments the company is announcing today, the company was able to use 13 hardware qubits to build a distance three color code, 37 for distance five, and 73 hardware qubits to get a distance seven logical qubit. These were then used to estimate the error rate that occurs when the logical qubits are simply used to hold onto the same state, essentially acting as a form of quantum memory. The performance of the hardware is good enough now, however, that just doing one round of error correction and measuring can’t provide an accurate measure of how often problems occur—errors are too rare. So instead, the team did 20 rounds of error correction before measuring to determine whether the memory had been maintained. To get this to work, the system had to take the syndrome data obtained from querying the measurement qubits and figure out the nature of any errors that were detected. As the distance of the error correction code goes up, it gets increasingly challenging to perform this analysis rapidly enough to keep it from becoming a bottleneck. The Quantinuum team showed that they had three different pieces of software, each able to operate in real time: a standard algorithm, a convolutional neural network, and a transformer-based neural network. For the distance three color code, the logical error rate was about 5 x 10 -4 . Stepping up to the distance five code brought that down to about 4 x 10 -5 , and the distance seven code saw another order-of-magnitude drop, down to 5 x 10 -6 . Overall, each step up in distance reduced the logical error rate by roughly a factor of 12. That is, to my knowledge, the best scaling seen yet. Another important step that was done here is showing that the syndrome data from one round only correlates with the data from the one immediately before and immediately after. This indicates that there are no systemic sources of error that are biasing the error-detection process. Of course, performing actual operations involves doing considerably more to the logical qubits than allowing them to just sit still and hold their state. So, the researchers also looked at the logical error rate associated with performing a relatively simple two-qubit gate operation. Unfortunately, this requires using two logical qubits, and the Helios processor isn’t able to hold more than one distance seven error code at a time. So instead, the researchers compared using hardware qubits directly and using distance three and five color codes. Running these two-qubit gates directly on the hardware produced an error rate of about 10 -3 , and the distance three code didn’t improve things dramatically. But the distance five code dropped the logical error rate to about 7 x 10 -5 . So, the hardware seems to be well beyond breakeven, even when it’s being asked to perform relatively complicated tasks. That other scaling These results can be viewed a couple of different ways. From the “no big deal” perspective, even the best logical error rate is still too high to perform complicated algorithms, and getting there had some major drawbacks: it was only seen when operations weren’t being performed on the qubit, and the system is only big enough to host one of these. We still have a long way to go before we’re ready to perform lots of error-corrected operations at a potentially useful error rate. From a more optimistic perspective, this is the best scaling I’m aware of, and the performance suggests that getting the hardware error rate down a bit further could have significant payoffs. The logical error rate depends on the hardware error rate in a way that means that, once things get good enough, then small improvements can have very large impacts on the logical error rate. The scaling seen here doesn’t tell us that we’re at that point, but it is suggestive that we’re getting close. The main question for Quantinuum is whether it can scale its qubit counts as effectively as its roadmap suggests it will. If so, it may not need to drop its hardware error rate much to start being able to generate useful logical qubits. That may mean solving somewhat different problems than some of its competitors, who will need to do different combinations of dropping the hardware error rate, boosting qubit counts, or figuring out how to integrate multiple functional units into a single computer. articles.content: The digital gold market itself is unlikely to move the overall demand dial much but is seen as an entry point into the wider bullion market, especially for younger investors who are obviously more wired than their older counterparts. By Ed Stoddard 20 Oct 2026 Digital gold eliminates the cumbersome logistics and settlement headaches associated with physical gold. (Photo: iStock) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper The digital gold market, worth about $50-billion today, is set for liftoff and could tap a swelling vein of demand to reach $700-billion, according to a new report by the World Gold Council (WGC) and Boston Consulting Group. Digital gold provides exposure to the precious metal through digital platforms, eliminating the cumbersome logistics and settlement headaches associated with physical gold. Gold is token reserve in BRICS de-dollarisation push As BRICS nations seek to break free from the dollar’s grip, a gold-backed digital currency could be the key to a new financial order. Can innovative token systems like Unit and the Standard Gold Unit create a stable, trusted alternative in the global marketplace? December 18, 2025 “As trading and record-keeping has moved onto electronic systems and markets have become more connected, investors have begun to expect gold to behave like other modern assets,” says the WGC. Traction is building on this front, bringing one of humanity’s oldest stores of wealth into the digital age. Token gesture “Momentum is already building as financial markets undergo a broader digital transformation, bringing tokenised investment products increasingly into the mainstream,” says the WGC. “Tokenised gold, one segment of the digital gold market alongside vaulted digital gold, has grown fivefold in value since late 2024 to around $6-billion. Cumulative spot trading volumes in tokenised gold exceeded $90-billion in the first quarter of 2026, more than in the whole of 2025.” This is still small potatoes. The current gold market is worth about $30-trillion at current prices and is focused on jewellery, bars, coins, gold-backed ETFs, OTC5 and central bank reserves. The physical investment gold market is worth about $13-trillion. The report sees digital gold growing to about $165-billion in the next five years, a figure that could reach $275-billion over the same timeframe if various barriers are removed. Source: World Gold Council. “What holds investors back is not a lack of interest but four key barriers: trust, access, utility and cost. Trust is the swing factor. Investors point to stronger consumer protections, transparent proof of backing, accessible redemption and clearer regulation as the conditions most likely to increase confidence in digital gold,” the WGC says. Access, meanwhile, is hampered by a lack of platforms outside of big Asian markets. “Where digital gold is embedded in mainstream channels such as super-apps, payment platforms and banking apps, as seen in India, China and Indonesia, penetration is up to seven times higher than in markets where such distribution does not yet exist.” The potential for a $700-billion market stems from “latent demand” – a pool of untapped investors who would rather do things in the digital space because this is the 21st century. “Among today’s digital gold investors, 52% held no gold before their first digital purchase, of which 92% have since bought other forms of gold,” says the report. Gold has been a red-hot commodity over the past few years and while it is off its historic peaks of almost $5,600 an ounce scaled in January this year, its price remains elevated at more than $4,000 an ounce. Performance enhancing A range of factors explain this performance, including geopolitical uncertainty – which enhances the precious metal’s safe-haven status – and central bank purchases, notably in emerging markets as the greenback loses some of its lustre as the world’s reserve currency. The digital gold market itself is unlikely to move the dial much on this front but is seen as an entry point into the wider bullion market, especially for younger investors who are obviously more wired than their older counterparts. Source: World Gold Council. “Around 65% of latent demand comes from people who have not yet invested in gold. Among those who already hold gold in other forms, more than half would fund a digital gold investment with money not currently allocated to the asset. “Rather than cannibalising demand for bars, coins or gold-backed ETFs, digital gold is thus likely to attract new investors, and new money,” the report says. articles.title: Frontline Ukrainian Forces Evacuate Wounded via Heavy Drone
articles.content: Every day, the Ukraine Battlefield update newsletter offers a clear look at how the war is unfolding on the ground. Subscribe for free here to get the full text delivered to your inbox. For the first time, Ukrainians rescued a wounded soldier by air. He spent 500 days at the front, during which he had to amputate his own legs. How the operation unfolded and what Ukrainians had to do to distract Russian drones. Rubio repeats Putin’s claims about occupied territory in the Donetsk region. Videos of the day: the first capture of a Russian tank this year; a swarm of Ukrainian drones. The information in this text is a summary of events on Monday (19 October). The situation may have changed since then. Hardly a week passes without some new development being reported on the frontline of Russia’s war in Ukraine. This time, Ukrainians demonstrated something truly unique. For the first time, they succeeded in evacuating a wounded soldier using a heavy rotary-wing aerial drone. The story was published by the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade and reported by a journalist from the Oboronka website , who spoke to both the operators and the wounded soldier. The evacuation took place near Kupiansk in the Kharkiv region, on the left, or eastern, bank of the Oskil river. Infantryman Kostiantyn ‘Magura’ Vlasenko of the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade was tasked, together with a comrade, with heading into the grey zone in early June 2025. Initially, they hid in one place, but when their position was flooded, they had to leave the building and take shelter elsewhere. Returning was impossible because of the dangerous situation. His comrade later died. In February this year, Magura was also wounded by a Russian drone. Munitions dropped from the drone injured both his legs. According to Oboronka , he had to amputate his own lower limbs in order to survive. The website did not give details of how he managed to do this. Similar cases have, however, occurred in the past. In 2018, for instance, during an exercise in Slovakia, an American soldier was trapped beneath a tank. He amputated his own leg to save a fellow soldier, for which he was named Soldier of the Year in 2021. In Magura's case, this meant he was left immobile, and it was clear that he would not return from the front by himself. Ukrainian units considered how to help him. Large language models trained on low-level assembly code translate compiled binary blobs directly into clean, human-readable source code. This eliminates the multi-month reverse engineering barrier that previously protected enterprise intellectual property and exposed zero-day hardware vulnerabilities.

articles.title: US State Lawmakers Legislate Against Foreign Transnational Repression
articles.content: Examining State-Level Legislation on Transnational Repression in the United States , Ted R. Bromund and Ariel Rawls Published on October 20, 2026 Transnational repression has become an increasingly visible public policy issue in the United States, and worldwide, over the past decade. The gruesome 2018 murder and dismemberment of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in the Saudi Consulate in Istanbul, the 2023 assassination of Canadian Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar outside of a British Columbia temple, and the 2025 rendition of Beninese journalist Comlan Hugues Sossoukpè from Côte d’Ivoire highlight the extent to which governments have brazenly targeted their nationals across borders. Initially, the policy response in the United States occurred entirely at the federal level. But over the past several years, U.S. states have begun to consider legislation on the issue. Not all of this legislation has been adopted, and the U.S. state-level response is clearly in an early phase. As U.S. states continue to respond to transnational repression, it is important that state legislators – and ultimately, members of Congress – understand what the states have done and what can be learned from their various approaches. One of the challenges of countering transnational repression is that it has not yet been defined in U.S. federal law. The democracy and rights organization Freedom House , which has played a leading role in drawing attention to the issue and in gathering data on it, defines transnational repression as “governments reaching across [national] borders to silence dissent among diaspora and exile communities.” (One of us, Grady, is a research analyst at Freedom House.) Perpetrator governments employ a range of tactics – including assassinations, illegal deportations, abductions, digital threats , and coercion-by-proxy – to intimidate and harass those who pose a perceived threat to the regime. Transnational repression can also involve the abuse by authoritarian regimes of legitimate international legal cooperation mechanisms such as Interpol’s notice system , mutual legal assistance frameworks and counterterrorism financing structures . The Federal Response The federal response to transnational repression in the United States has been varied . Numerous congressional committees have held hearings — including multiple hearings by the U.S. Helsinki Commission and most recently, and relevantly, the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) June 4, 2026, hearing on “The PRC’s Threats to Americans: Transnational Repression & State-Level Responses.” Federal law enforcement has regularly brought cases against perpetrators, and U.S. congressional offices have introduced several bills on transnational repression, including the Transnational Repression Policy Act (TRPA). Yet, that bipartisan and bicameral legislation, which would codify a formal definition of the phenomenon into law and mandate the development of a government strategy to blunt the threat, has struggled to move on the Hill, given other legislative priorities. U.S. administrations have also evaded the intent of the most significant U.S. legislation, Section 6503 of the 2022 National Defense Authorization Act, entitled “Transnational Repression Accountability and Prevention” or “ TRAP .” The provisions directed the Attorney General and Secretary of State to provide biannual reports to Congress on authoritarian governments’ misuse of Interpol’s systems, support reforms to prevent such abuse, and develop a coordinated U.S. response to this form of transnational repression. While the required initial report was submitted in August 2022, the TRAP provisions have not produced the sustained reporting, coordinated implementation, or broader accountability that Congress envisioned. The result is that, while the U.S. federal government has done more than any other government to raise awareness about transnational repression, its response has been neither unified nor consistent. Indeed, the United States and other democracies continue to facilitate transnational repression via their immigration and extradition systems by detaining and deporting dissidents. Part of the challenge is that, precisely because of the widespread participation of democracies in international legal cooperation, it is all too easy for perpetrator governments to abuse these systems to seek the return of exiled activists and dissidents. While those mechanisms require greater transparency and stronger safeguards against abuse, receiving countries must also ensure that they do not detain, extradite, or deport individuals based solely on uncorroborated allegations or requests from governments with a documented history of abusing these systems for political purposes. By the same token, a great deal of transnational repression occurs outside of immigration enforcement, in the everyday lives of those targeted. Adhering to due process standards when adjudicating claims for asylum, while essential, will not protect individuals from surveillance, harassment, coercion, or intimidation by foreign regimes or their agents inside the United States. These are acts that can be addressed at the state level. Indeed, given the federal structure of the United States, leaving every offense to the federal government to criminalize is neither sensible nor safe. U.S. states, in addition to serving as legislative laboratories, can play a constructive role in responding to the challenge of transnational repression. State Legislative History and Legal Mechanisms In recent years, state legislatures have increasingly taken steps to address foreign interference. In general, legislative initiatives have been broad, treating transnational repression, alongside land sales and foreign lobbying campaigns , as increasingly serious national security concerns. These broad approaches have prompted some concerns about the potential for overreach. At a June hearing of the U.S House of Representatives Select Committee on China, the president of Asian Americans Advancing Justice, John C. Yang, cautioned that efforts to address foreign interference must avoid repeating historical instances of national security concerns leading to ethnicity-based suspicion rather than evidence-based enforcement. Since the beginning of 2025, seven states have adopted laws that explicitly mention transnational repression and enact measures to respond to the phenomenon. While these laws vary to some extent in scope and approach, they reflect growing state-level attention to the problem. In May 2025, Texas became the first state to pass legislation to counter transnational repression. Senate Bill 1349 , signed into law by Governor Greg Abbott on May 24, 2025, and effective on September 1, 2025, criminalizes actions committed by a foreign government or terrorist organization, or an agent working on behalf of these entities, when the acts interfere with Texas residents’ protected conduct under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution or in some way coerce a Texas resident to either work for a foreign principal or to leave the United States . The law also makes it illegal to enforce another country’s laws in the state. The sentencing enhancement for serving a foreign principal can be applied to pre-existing offenses in the Texas penal code, including assault, stalking, and human trafficking. The law also requires the Texas Department of Public Safety to create a training program for Texas law enforcement on common tactics and on the primary perpetrators of transnational repression, and requires the Department, in collaboration with the Governor’s office, to prepare a study on the issue. While the law identifies how transnational repression infringes on the rights of affected individuals, it takes an overly expansive view of the perpetrators by including terrorist organizations. Unlike terrorist offenses, which usually attack state institutions or the public at large, government-directed campaigns are targeted against particular private individuals who, as individuals, have the rights the law seeks to protect. Moreover, the act incorrectly implies that terrorist organizations stably control territory and are recognized foreign principals. Soon after Texas passed its law in 2025, Nebraska adopted the Crush Transnational Repression in Nebraska Act . It defines transnational repression as actions committed by a foreign government or terrorist organization, or an agent working on behalf of these entities, “with the intention of harassing, intimidating, censoring, or otherwise extending such principal’s ability to influence, control, or impose such principal’s preferences on the behavior of individuals outside of the principal’s territory or jurisdiction.” Similarly to the Texas measure, the Nebraska law introduces a criminal sentencing enhancement for covered offenses — including first-, second- and third-degree assault, stalking, and violation of a harassment protection order, among others — that interfere with Nebraskans’ protected conduct under the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution or that seek to force a Nebraska resident to work for a foreign principal or leave the United States. In addition to these increased penalties, the act calls on Nebraska State Patrol to create training on cross-border repression tactics and key perpetrators, to establish a website with a multilingual reporting mechanism for targeted individuals, and to prepare a report for the legislature. Certainly, training and multilingual reporting tools are helpful. However, the legislation’s repeated reference to the term “foreign adversary” may increase the likelihood that the implementation process will only focus on governments like China and Iran and overlook transnational repression linked to U.S. allies such as Saudi Arabia and India . Laws in Arizona (2025), Kansas (2026), Louisiana (2026), and Tennessee (2026) share very similar descriptions of transnational repression and policy prescriptions with the legislation approved in Texas and Nebraska. Each of these four states have enshrined in law additional criminal penalties for those acting on behalf of a foreign government or terrorist organization to infringe upon the First Amendment rights of state residents or coerce an individual to serve a foreign government or terrorist group. The four also call for training and awareness-raising programs for law enforcement and, in the case of Tennessee, other state agencies. These laws could serve to heighten awareness of trends and tactics, but like the other states, they risk misdiagnosing the threat by including terrorist groups as perpetrators. Likewise, the use of “foreign adversary” in the Kansas, Louisiana, and Tennessee laws may shift attention away from the rights of all targeted diaspora members and result in states employing the legislation primarily to focus on geopolitical foes of the United States. Other legislation specifically tasks higher education institutions with protecting students on their campuses from foreign threats. Kansas’s legislation acknowledges the existence of the threat at higher education institutions and directs the University of Kansas and Kansas State University to incorporate information on transnational repression in disciplinary policies and designate a university office or representative to receive complaints. International students and staff often face resistance from their co-nationals who disagree with criticisms of their homeland government or disapprove of events dedicated to human rights issues in the perpetrator country. A March 2026 law in Utah contains a sentencing-enhancement tool for those acting on behalf of foreign governments or terrorist organizations to compel or prevent certain behaviors, and obligates the Utah Department of Higher Education to advise international students of the threat of transnational repression and how to report possible incidents to local law enforcement. Such efforts to provide resources to students, who are often among the most vulnerable and targeted members of diasporas, help promote academic freedom. As these universities roll out bodies to review possible incidents, it is important that those on campus accused of performing such acts on behalf of a foreign government are also afforded due process. Not all legislative projects related to transnational repression have received the assent of governors upon making it out of statehouses. California Senate Bill 509 , which passed through both chambers of the state legislature in 2025, tasked the California Office of Emergency Services (OES) with instituting a transnational repression recognition and response training for state and local law enforcement and first responders. The bill notably lacked reference to individual governments that have sought to silence U.S.-based individuals. However, divisions quickly emerged within and across diaspora communities over the ramifications of the prospective initiative. A broad coalition of groups representing Sikh, Indian Muslim, Indian Hindu, and Iranian communities — all of which have sizable populations in California and have faced increasing transnational repression in North America — argued that the bill would make community members feel safer by raising awareness among police officers. Conversely, other diaspora advocacy organizations such as the Coalition of Hindus of North America and the Hindu American Foundation contended that the legislation would unfairly lead law enforcement to stereotype Hindu Americans as foreign agents. Governor Gavin Newsom ultimately vetoed the bill in October 2025 on the grounds that the state must coordinate closely with federal agencies on codifying definitions and training guidelines and that the OES had already launched a training program for officers. Somewhat analogous logic underpinned Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers’ decision to not sign a transnational repression bill in March 2026. The legislation, Wisconsin Assembly Bill 672 , would have established a penalty enhancer like those in other approved laws for anyone operating on behalf of foreign governments or terrorist organizations. It also would have required the Wisconsin Department of Justice to develop a mechanism for reporting cases and a training program for law enforcement. Evers justified his veto by arguing that foreign affairs and international relations fall under the purview of the federal government. The governor further highlighted that the state’s criminal code already prohibits the offenses described in the bill and contains a hate crimes penalty enhancer, and that the legislature had not appropriated sufficient resources for the implementation of the legislation. The American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee applauded this rejection and registered concern that the bill’s vague language could have enabled the silencing of dissent from certain communities. Guidelines for Future State-Level Legislation It is too early to assess the successes (or failures) of state-level legislation on transnational repression and whether these laws are making diaspora activists and journalists safer in the United States. Most states have only considered legislation, not passed it, and even the legislation that has been passed has not been in operation long enough to evaluate. But it is not too early, based on prior research on transnational repression and legislative approaches to it, to set out guidelines for future state-level legislation in the United States. Legislation Should Focus on Intent, Not Specific Tactics One of the most frustrating things about transnational repression is how rapidly it evolves. Authoritarian regimes are quick to capitalize on new technology , explore new avenues of repression, and copy one another after an initial success. The initial abuse of the Interpol Red Notice system, for example, rapidly transitioned into exploitation of Blue Notices and Interpol’s passport database . Counterterrorism financing measures were exploited almost as quickly. Regimes are able to bypass country-based controls by acting in collaboration with one another, as Belarus is accused of doing with Russia . New venues for transnational repression open up regularly: there is, for example, vastly more concern now about it in U.S. higher education than there was a decade ago. All of this suggests that legislation that is focused on one avenue for transnational repression, one location of it, or one national perpetrator will rapidly be outdated. Even if concern about the issue results mostly from concern about one country, the best legislation will be general, focusing on the actions and intents of perpetrators in general. Foreign Terrorist Organizations Should Not Be Listed as Perpetrators Grouping foreign terrorist organizations with foreign governments as perpetrators of transnational repression, as most existing state-level laws do, complicates the implementation of responses and risks infringing upon the rights of individuals in the United States from foreign countries. Many governments weaponize the label of terrorism against targeted individuals to legitimize efforts to intimidate or capture them. Targeted individuals faced terrorism or extremism accusations in about 46 percent of the 1,375 incidents of physical, direct transnational repression identified by Freedom House from 2014 to 2025, according to the organization’s nonpublic dataset. By incorporating vague descriptions of terrorism in legislation, states make it easier for foreign governments to camouflage their politically motivated pursuit of certain individuals to state-level officials who may be less familiar with the contexts related to the countries of origin. Transnational Repression Is Not Primarily a National Security Issue The prestige (and funding) that attaches to issues that are defined as relevant to national security naturally leads advocates to want to define lots of concerns as national security issues. This is understandable and may help place the phenomenon on the agenda of lawmakers, but it does not capture the unique impacts of transnational repression on individuals. On an abstract level, transnational repression involves foreign nations carrying out actions inside the United States that violate U.S. sovereignty, and thus can reasonably be called a national security concern. But on a concrete level, most transnational repression is more akin to violations of privacy, stalking, harassment, or attempted acts of violence than it is to espionage — which is in any case already criminalized at the federal level. While the enacted state-level laws refer to these offenses under penal codes, accompanying press releases and the June CECC hearing connect their passage with broader campaigns to blunt foreign interference in institutions. Opposing transnational repression is fundamentally about defending individuals’ rights guaranteed by the Bill of Rights. If the perspective of sovereignty helps lawmakers understand the issue, it is useful. However, advancing transnational repression legislation alongside initiatives that tackle other forms of foreign interference (espionage, intellectual property theft, election interference, and lobbying) downplays the everyday harassment of exiled activists and diaspora leaders. Legislation Should Be Actor-Agnostic State laws’ text and their sponsors often pin the problem on “foreign adversaries” as defined by 15 CFR Section 791.4 . Such countries include China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and Venezuela. This narrow, geopolitical framing risks ignoring such incidents carried out by notable U.S. allies, including Egypt, India, Rwanda, and Saudi Arabia. The targeting of American citizens and permanent residents such as Sikh political activist Gurpantwant Singh Pannun by India, Rwandan dissident Paul Rusesabagina by his home government, and Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi by the Saudi regime highlights the disregard these governments have for their nationals’ ties to the United States. Focusing only on U.S. rivals reinforces a national security approach that overlooks how transnational repression violates the rights of diaspora members from a diverse range of countries. Encourage Reporting and Training Current state-level legislation promotes training for law enforcement and, in some cases, reporting of transnational repression. These two go hand-in-hand. First responders must have an awareness of the tactics employed by prominent perpetrator governments, and targeted individuals must have the opportunity to report possible incidents in their own languages. State-level law enforcement could follow the example of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, which has published warnings in Punjabi — although after the recent arrests in California and elsewhere of individuals linked to Indian organized crime and the 2023 assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada, both the FBI and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California notably refused to comment on issues around transnational repression , perhaps because raising the issue of transnational repression would directly implicate the Indian government, a U.S. ally. States considering legislation can encourage reporting by creating contact points not only in police departments but also in state and local governments that readily follow up on previous engagements with affected individuals. Individuals may not feel comfortable sharing details with law enforcement due to negative experiences with security services in their homeland or concerns over their immigration status. Thus, institutional liaisons – as Kansas legislation offers university students – may foster improved reporting by targeted immigrants. Conclusion The rise of state-level legislation on transnational repression illustrates how U.S. states are laboratories of democracy. To date, seven states have adopted laws in advance of the federal government. And, in most instances, the states learn from, or copy from, other states: much of the state-level legislation is very similar. It would take an in-depth legislative history to reveal the flow of influence from state to state, but the commonalities of this legislation emphasize how important it is to legislate wisely: state-level legislation can have an influence far beyond the borders of a single state. Whether state-level legislation is the right or wrong approach is ultimately for the states to decide. If state-level legislation can build further awareness of transnational repression and if it can play any role at all in protecting the lives and rights of individuals in the United States, it will have served a useful purpose. articles.title: Google Public Sector Launches Sovereign Gemini for Governments
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Christian Robles , Technology Reporter, Nextgov/FCW | October 20, 2026 06:00 AM ET Agencies already have discounted access to Gemini through Nov. 15 under a OneGov deal. Industry Google Public Sector on Tuesday unveiled Gemini for government services — an add-on that gives federal, state and local governments access to specialized skills, artificial intelligence agents and integrations with frequently used software. The suite of tools can help government officials interpret dense regulations, redact documents requested through the Freedom of Information Act, translate jargony documents into simple language and review contracting bids, in addition to completing other tasks, according to a company press release. Select agencies, including the federal Health and Human Services Department and the State of Missouri, have been testing Gemini for government services over the past few weeks, Chris Hein, field CTO at Google Public Sector, told Nextgov/FCW . The company is accepting additional early adopters of Gemini for government services to field feedback before general availability is expected later this year, he added. There is no target date for general availability. “Gemini for government services provides a secure environment for agencies to automate workflows, allowing civil servants to focus on delivering the responsive, high-quality services that citizens expect,” said Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, in the release. Gemini for government services includes pre-built, specialized skills that serve as a set of rules instructing Gemini to execute a task without going off script, Hein told Nextgov/FCW. Government officials can refer to a skill in the Gemini prompt bar that would help analyze regulations, audit expenses and conduct other activities, according to a video demo . Officials can also access third-party AI agents from other companies, such as Accenture Federal Services and Deloitte, to further assist government work, the release says. Google Public Sector will “prescreen” the AI agents, which agency IT leadership, not individual users, can enable through a behind-the-scenes portal, Hein explained to Nextgov/FCW . Some agents are already available but most are not yet, he added. Gemini for government services includes secure connections to technologies officials already use, such as Google Workspace, Microsoft SharePoint, Outlook 365, Salesforce and ServiceNow, the release says. That connector feature extends to federal regulations by digital services company BLEN, allowing officials to search the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, regulations.gov and the Federal Register. The feature includes a connection to Oracle enterprise apps, according to the release. When Gemini for government services achieves general availability, agency IT leadership will be able to choose which connections they want to enable for which set of users, Hein said. In the demo, a compliance analyst for a state chief information security officer used Gemini for government services to analyze federal cybersecurity regulations with the pre-built policy and statute assistant skill. After the analysis, the user asked Gemini to draft a ServiceNow incident ticket to remediate contracts for compliance with the federal cybersecurity rules. The user could edit the incident ticket before sending it. Federal agencies have access to Gemini for $0.47 per agency per year through Nov. 15 under a recently extended OneGov deal . Share This:

articles.title: Boeing Secures Critical FAA Clearance for Delayed Max Ten Jetliner
articles.summary: Boeing obtained FAA regulatory approval to commence formal certification flight testing for its delayed 737 Max 10 jetliner, marking a pivotal milestone in its grueling corporate rehabilitation effort. The approval provides a desperately needed commercial lifeline as Boeing works to prevent major airline customers from canceling billions of dollars in backlogged orders and switching to Airbus. However, intense regulatory scrutiny and strict manufacturing quality audits will significantly extend the timeline before the aircraft enters passenger service.
articles.deck: Boeing secures FAA testing approval for Max 10, delivering a vital lifeline to its turnaround.
bullets: Federal Aviation Administration cleared Boeing to initiate official certification flight tests for the 737 Max 10.
Milestone follows years of delays triggered by engineering revisions, software redesigns, and regulatory mandates.
The Max 10 is Boeing's primary narrowbody weapon to counter the market-dominating Airbus A321neo.
Financial Times World reported major airline carriers retain hundreds of conditional advance purchase orders.

Every month of certification delay costs Boeing hundreds of millions in penalty payments to furious airline customers. Intensified FAA scrutiny means aviation safety standards are finally taking precedence over quarterly corporate profits. articles.title: Texas Pushes Data Center Approvals Despite Promised Statewide Permit Halt
articles.content: • 'It Ain't Right:' Texas Said It Would Halt Data Center Permits. The State is Pushing Ahead Anyway · Oct 19, 2026 at 5:40 PM “The Caldwell Technology Park [...] the Stargate facility, and a bunch of other very large hyperscale facilities have gotten regulatory approvals [...] so it's not like a real pause." A group of Texans believe they’ve discovered evidence that the state’s environmental regulatory agency has continued to issue permits to data centers despite Governor Greg Abbott’s call for it to stop.  The nonprofits Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance, working with local activists in Texas, looked through the public database of the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) and discovered that the organization has worked on multiple permits for data center projects since Abbott called for a pause in the process on September 21. Abbott’s office denied approving any new permits in a statement to 404 Media.  According to Public Citizen and the FracTracker Alliance, which cite documents publicly available on the TCEQ’s website, the agency has reviewed documents and assigned engineers related to more than a dozen permits related to data center projects in the state. Public Citizen listed more than 15 and the Fractracker Alliance found 35 . The same day the nonprofits announced their findings, The Texas Tribune published a report that Abbott had received $9 million in donations from developers and owners of data centers. According to the documents reviewed by 404 Media, TCEQ issued air-emission limit certificates to a large data center in Houston; approved the construction of stormwater coverage for data centers in Abilene , Barstow , and Royse City ; and fast tracked gas power plants for more than a dozen data center projects. “The TCEQ’s own data indicates that it’s business as usual for data centers and affected communities were promised a freeze. And instead what they’re getting is another reason to distrust the TCEQ and ultimately ineffective attempts to govern by press release,” Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen said during a press conference on Monday about the findings. “Absent any comprehensive guardrails imposed by the Texas legislature, the industry will continue to move forward as fast as it can, and the TCEQ may let it.” "They're still putting in that power plant, and there ain't nothing me and my people can do about it. We're just going to have to keep that boot on our neck. It ain’t right.” Texas is poised to be the data center capital of the world. Three hundred already operate in the state, 100 are under construction, and 200 more are being planned . The projects include Big Tech companies like Meta — which is constructing a $14 billion data center in El Paso — smaller scale local projects like one in Taylor that would be built on land meant for a public park, and massive startups like the nuclear-powered Fermi data center in Amarillo. In general, people hate data centers and it’s become a major political issue for voters in Texas. On September 21, Abbott directed the TCEQ to “halt all permits sought by data centers.”   Abbott said he’d told the state’s water and electric utility agencies to audit all the projects and directed “the TCEQ to pause the issuance of all permits related to data center projects until [the Electric Reliability Council of Texas] completes its review.” Abbott’s order is broad and data centers are large and complicated construction projects with a lot of moving parts that require dozens of permits and plans. It’s possible that some of the permits uncovered by the nonprofits were filed before Abbott’s September 21 pause. Many, however, were clearly issued afterward. Twelve of the 14 applications for gas plants and generators were filed in October. TCEQ used an expedited review process for eight of them. One was an air permit for engines and turbines that would power a data center in the Dallas suburb of Irving, Texas . The builder submitted the permit for expedited review on October 6 and a TCEQ engineer completed the initial review two days later, according to publicly available documents reviewed by 404 Media. “No permits have been approved,” Governor Abbot’s press secretary Andrew Mahaleris told 404 Media. “In line with the Governor’s directive, TCEQ has not taken and will not take any proactive actions related to the approval of data center permits. Likewise, no other state agency will approve data center-related permits until the Public Utility Commission, ERCOT, and the Water Development Board have the information they need to make informed decisions. Texans must come first.” 404 Media asked Abbott’s office why there are multiple data center related stormwater construction projects listed as “approved” and was told to talk to TCEQ. "The Commission has not issued any permits related to data centers and is complying with Governor Abbott’s directive," TCEQ told 404 Media. 💡 Do you know anything else about this story? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at +1 347 762-9212 or send me an email at matthew@404media.co. Sam Law, a researcher and manager of communications at FracTracker Alliance, told 404 Media that TCEQ gave him “a more exacting interpretation of their own situation,” he said. “Which is that they are accepting applications, but not moving forward with reviewing them. That was shown to not be true.” Law also noted that the stormwater construction permits that read as “approved” in the TCEQ system are the result of a regulatory loophole. “The state has just approved a generic construction stormwater permit, and then to get onto that permit, people file a notice of intent and then they add them to a pre-existing permit,” Law said. The stormwater construction permit is required to raise and level ground. “It’s often the final approval needed to move forward to prepare the site to actually build the physical structure," he added. In areas where there’s no zoning restrictions or the city is unincorporated, then that permit is all a company needs to start building. “The Caldwell Technology Park [...] the Stargate facility, and a bunch of other very large hyperscale facilities have gotten regulatory approvals in the form of this notice of intent, so it's not like a real pause,” he said. Law said he believes Abbott is trying to project opposition to data centers without doing the real regulatory work. “If the point of the pause is to stop the sort of approvals of data centers, that's not what's been happening,” he said. 0:00 / 2:27 1× Multiple data center projects are underway in Abilene, Texas — including OpenAI’s Stargate project. According to TCEQ’s records, it issued a water quality permit for the Abilene data center on September 23. “We are, in fact, going to get a massive gas turbine plant right to people’s houses,” Abilene resident and Democratic state senate candidate Riley Rodriquez said during Public Citizen’s press conference. Rodriquez said that residents had gotten letters from TCEQ about the incoming gas plant and how it might affect air quality in the region. The people of Abilene have fought and won the right to testify at upcoming public hearings .  “At the end of the day they’re going to flip that switch. Doesn't matter what we have to say at that public hearing, and I know that is a doom and gloom way to look at this. But that's the fact,” Rodriquez said. “The fact of the matter is, we can go to that. We can have the best comments. We can have the best information [...] and I could have 500,000 people behind me, and it doesn't matter because they're going to flip that switch because they put the money on it anyways. And we got to live with that  — with those consequences.”  Rodriquez said the people of the region found out about Stargate too late to do anything about it. “We're in a unique situation for us because we didn't have a chance to do any of the things that these great people are doing. We didn't have a chance to do any of that. ‘It was built, concrete's poured, generators are going in, boys. Sorry,’” he said. “So Abbott made his announcement. That's really great, that's really awesome,” Rodriquez said. “Guess what? They're still putting in that power plant, and there ain't nothing me and my people can do about it. We're just going to have to keep that boot on our neck. It ain’t right.” In his September 21 letter, Abbott said he’d ordered the pause because “the goal is to put Texans first.” Update 10/19/26 at 8:20PM: This story has been updated to include a response from TCEQ . Matthew Gault is a writer covering weird tech, nuclear war, and video games. He’s worked for Reuters, Motherboard, and the New York Times. More from Matthew Gault • •
