articles.title: Morgan Stanley Identifies $1.6 Trillion Electrical Chokepoints Strangling AI
articles.content: By Morgan Stanley’s count, 91.7% of Nvidia’s 2027 revenue is exposed to one thing: AI infrastructure demand. No company on the bank’s list scores higher. Not Vertiv , at 90%. Not Broadcom , at 81%. Recommended Video The same report, published Oct. 15, calls Nvidia the best risk/reward in the sector. The bull case for the world’s most valuable company and the bull case for the build-out are now essentially the same case, and Morgan Stanley’s North America Insight, led by Nicholas Lentini, makes both. The note, titled Following AI’s $1.6 Trillion Money Trail: Mapping the Revenue Generated by the Capex Boom, includes a section that runs under the heading “We Are Bullish This Spend.” The 65-page note also spends a good part of its length explaining how the spending could break. Nvidia’s defenders would say that exposure describes the company. Its data center business has supplied the large majority of its revenue for years, but the report adds a closer look on how few buyers that exposure runs through. The firm estimates hyperscalers and AI cloud providers will spend $1.58 trillion in 2027, up roughly 60% from about $980 billion this year, and will spend $1.8 trillion in 2028. About $195 billion of the 2027 figure is data center leases, which never show up as capital spending on a cash flow statement. The report calls leases “synthetic capex.” Hyperscalers have disclosed more than $1.1 trillion in lease commitments that haven’t started yet. About $1 trillion of the 2027 spending lands as S&P 500 revenue, by Morgan Stanley’s estimate. Nearly $700 billion of it goes to Nvidia. Revenue from hyperscaler and neocloud customers makes up 5% of total S&P 500 revenue in 2027 but drives about 25% of the index’s revenue growth. Nvidia’s own customer list is even narrower. In the bank’s model, SpaceX and Amazon Web Services together account for about 54% of Nvidia’s hyperscaler revenue in 2027 and 72% of its growth. Morgan Stanley’s argument is that Nvidia is cheap for what it is. The stock trades at 15 times fiscal 2028 earnings, and the bank says multiple expansion “is also not required for the stock to work as numbers continue to go higher.” It expects the spending to earn 25% to 50% on invested capital. It also argues Wall Street has underestimated compute cycles by 38%, on average, based on four past cycles: PCs, the internet, mobile, and cloud. The bank even says its own Nvidia numbers may be low. It calls its SpaceX and Amazon estimates conservative, creating “a low bar for remaining hyperscalers.” Its model has Nvidia’s share of the other hyperscalers’ spending slipping from 18% in 2026 to 16% in 2027. Nvidia expects to gain share. Other parts of the company have sounded less certain. In March, Morgan Stanley’s global investment committee said the bull market “rests, more than anything, on the durability of AI capital expenditures.” The report’s risk section reads like a list of everything the 91.7% depends on. Money comes first. Morgan Stanley expects 2027 to bring the largest cash flow deficit of its forecast period, and with it more debt. Hyperscalers have already sold about $255 billion of unsecured bonds this year, roughly 30% of estimated 2026 spending. In what the bank calls a theoretical exercise, it models the cost of borrowing more. Amazon, Alphabet , Meta , and Microsoft , rated AA or higher, see combined interest coverage fall from about 31x to 12x. Oracle and SpaceX fall from 4x to 1.8x. Some of the spending growth is inflation. A meaningful part of recent capex increases reflects higher component prices, according to the report. It cites Amazon’s finance chief attributing most of an increase in Amazon’s spending plan, from $200 billion to about $220 billion, to rising memory costs, with no change to the build plan. Then there’s power. The $1.6 trillion assumes every chip ordered gets switched on. Morgan Stanley’s own power model projects a 32-gigawatt U.S. shortfall for data centers through 2028, about one-third of the 97 gigawatts needed. The report notes that hyperscalers can keep buying scarce GPUs ahead of power, which would hold up chip revenue for a while and “could produce hoarding and stranded inventory.” “But buying power-dependent equipment that cannot be turned on is hard to sustain,” it says. Politics is last. The firm calls data center restrictions a wedge issue in the midterms. It doesn’t expect a federal pause, but it sees tax breaks as “the consensus target regardless of who wins.” Morgan Stanley’s downside case is a timing problem. If spending plateaus, it argues, volumes can hold up while prices fall, and suppliers’ margins disappear first. The bank points to the late-2022 memory downturn, when NAND shipments fell only about 5% while prices fell 20% to 30%. The bank argues Nvidia would be spared the worst. In a pause, it writes, “we’re likely to see the most disruption at the tail of the bullwhip,” in memory, optics, and other small-dollar parts most likely to be over-ordered. By the report’s own map, Nvidia sits at the other end of the whip as the single largest supplier in the chain. The same report that says Wall Street underestimates compute cycles by 38% also says Wall Street “is underprepared for the depth of cuts to the downside.” The risk of volume and price falling together, it says, is underappreciated. “It’s the standard capital-cycle playbook,” the report says, “just compressed by how concentrated the hyperscaler customer base is.” Generative AI was used for research assistance and/or transcription of this article. articles.title: European Defense Spending Fragmentation Undermines Joint Military Procurement
articles.content: Europe is supposed to be financing its defence together. It barely is. Of the €800bn announced under ReArm Europe in March 2025, €650bn is not common money. It is an estimate of the extra room governments get under the national escape clause to spend up to 1.5 percent of GDP more on defence for four years. Each country still pays for that spending itself. The room is also temporary: EU Commission simulations suggest that maintaining higher defence spending after 2028 could require additional annual fiscal adjustment of 0.25 to 0.4 percentage points of GDP from 2029. The other €150bn is SAFE , and it is loans, not grants. The EU borrows and lends the money on, and each country repays its share. Grants are small: €1.5bn from the European Defence Industry Programme for 2025-2027, plus the European Defence Fund for joint research. Not every country has used these tools, as Table 1 shows. The Netherlands and Sweden have used neither. Like Germany, which has taken only the clause, they can borrow at least as cheaply as the EU, so SAFE gets them nothing. France has taken SAFE but not the clause, to protect the credibility of its budget plans. Table 1. Who uses SAFE and the national escape clause Source: Council of the EU, European Commission. Data as of 17 October 2026. * Hungary: allocated €16.2bn, now requesting €5.4bn; still pending. ** Italy: the Commission backed its request on 8 October 2026; the Council has yet to decide. Where SAFE does matter is on the eastern flank. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia can borrow the equivalent of five to eight percent of their GDP, and Poland almost five percent. Graph 1. SAFE loans as a share of GDP, by country (%) Source: Council of the EU, European Commission, Eurostat. SAFE loans only, as a share of 2025 GDP. Amounts approved by the Council, except Italy and Hungary (* revised requests of €8bn and €5.4bn, September 2026). Data as of 17 October 2026. That leaves private money. The European Investment Bank and the European Investment Fund are trying to bring in private investors, partly by removing the reputational stigma of financing defence. But defence is almost a monopsony: the state is nearly the only buyer. Without a clear flow of public orders, private investment will be hard to come by. So Europe barely borrows together. The exhibition features nearly 120 mainstream domestic and international automobile brands showcasing approximately 1,600 vehicles under the theme "Leading the Trend, Moving Towards the New." (Photo by An Yuan/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images)China News Service | China News Service | Getty ImagesGlobal automakers face an increasingly demanding customer: one who wants both competitive prices and better technology, according to Bain & Company. Tech and features were a leading purchase consideration for 58% of Chinese consumers, ranking ahead of price, the consultancy's latest Global Automotive Consumer Survey found. In the U.S. and Europe, price remained the top consideration, cited by 68% and 62%, respectively. However, that does not mean Chinese buyers have stopped caring about affordability. Intense domestic competition has made low prices an expectation in China, pushing carmakers to stand out through technology and features, Bain executives told CNBC. Stricker expects Western markets to follow, with competitive pricing becoming a baseline and technology playing a bigger role in purchasing decisions. Moreover, growing competition from Chinese manufacturers is expected to intensify pricing pressure in Europe, he added. China’s vehicle exports to Italy more than doubled to 209,258 units in January-August, while U.K. shipments rose about 86% to 365,672, according to customs figures cited by the China Passenger Car Association. Meanwhile, weakening brand loyalty threatens an advantage established manufacturers have relied on for decades. "European manufacturers [have] basically based their business model for decades on brand loyalty," Stricker said, but that allegiance is fading. More than a third of customers in Western markets are open to new brands entering the market, Bain's survey found. Buyers most interested in autonomous-driving technology are also more willing to switch manufacturers for better functionality. Helen Liu, Asia automotive head and partner at Bain, said that younger U.S. and European consumers are closer to Chinese buyers in their openness to technology, adding that Western manufacturers need to "up their game" to retain those customers. But monetizing those features could prove difficult. While Stricker said that mass-market buyers often expected advanced driving technology to be included rather than carry a substantial premium, Liu added that those demands leave Chinese and Western manufacturers "climbing different mountains." Emerging Chinese players must build their brand standing, while Western incumbents must strengthen their technology offerings. All players must keep prices competitive. Manufacturers that can close their respective gaps without pricing themselves out of buyers' consideration stand to gain the most as the industry consolidates, according to Bain. – CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this story.

articles.title: Federal Legislation Empowers US Citizens to Sue ICE for Wrongful Detention
articles.content: What Happened: A New Mexico Democrat in the House introduced a bill last week that would make it easier for U.S. citizens to sue immigration agents and the federal government over wrongful detentions and arrests. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández credited ProPublica’s reporting as the catalyst for the bill, the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act. Earlier this month, we revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained in warrantless arrests during the second Trump administration. Leger Fernández said the legislation would roll back the protections from lawsuits that agents and the federal government currently have. It would also establish a minimum level of compensation for people who win their suits, and extend the statute of limitations for such cases. The legislation would also take back any unspent Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding from President Donald Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Leger Fernández’s bill was introduced with co-sponsor Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, a New Jersey Democrat. Why It Matters: It can be difficult to sue federal officers for wrongful arrests or excessive force, or for local prosecutors to bring charges . Federal agents can claim immunity in response to civil lawsuits or to state charges and can move their cases to federal court. People who accuse immigration agents of wrongdoing can currently only sue in a narrow set of circumstances, and p revious Democratic bills aiming to change that have not passed. Some local prosecutors have announced investigations into the wrongful arrests of U.S. citizens or prosecuted federal agents accused of wrongdoing during immigration enforcement actions. What They Said: In an interview with ProPublica, Leger Fernández emphasized that accountability could not only address past wrongs, it may also help head them off in the future. “We know that when there are consequences, bad actors start behaving better because they don’t want to face those consequences,” she said. Without legislation, Leger Fernández said, agents “will continue to violate the law, to violate their own policy, and to violate the Constitution without any consequences.” Asked about the legislation, the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, repeated claims that it is not arresting U.S. citizens and defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.” Background: The federal government denies that there is any pattern of immigration agents detaining U.S. citizens, but according to ProPublica’s count, more than 100 citizens were held after agents questioned their citizenship. At least 70 children and teens were also detained. Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens after our earlier investigation found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents . The government and National Taiwan University’s Department of Civil Engineering trained the AI tool on 8,000 images of quake-damaged buildings taken in Taiwan and abroad, the National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering (NCREE) told a news conference. The tool uses images to generate a suggested structural damage severity rating to aid engineers, said Tsai Hung-yin (蔡宏營), president of the National Institutes of Applied Research, which oversees the center. The powerful quake in Tainan and Chiayi last year that damaged 4,291 buildings revealed the need to improve efficiency in performing post-tremor damage assessments necessary for reconstruction, he said. The AI model makes preliminary assessments in one second, compared with 30 seconds to a minute a human evaluator requires, NCREE Director Ou Yu-chen (歐昱辰) said. Certified structural engineers who use the tool are 15 times faster than their unassisted colleagues in evaluating building damage, Ou said. A publicly available version of the tool, called “safe and seismic-resistant home AI” (安全耐震我的AI), would enable ordinary people to estimate their structure’s ability to withstand earthquakes using pictures of their home’s structural walls, pillars and beams, he said. Should the AI assess a structure to be unsafe, it would recommend that the user contacts certified technicians, he said. The tool is expected to be launched on the center’s Web site by the end of this week. The model allows engineers to make damage assessments at once, eliminating the redundant travel for reassessments that accounts for the bulk of time wastage, NCREE associate researcher Chang Wei-tze (張慰慈) said. The public version classifies structural components into three categories: severe damage, indicating danger; moderate damage, requiring caution; and minor damage or no obvious damage, Chang said. He said people should think of the tool as being similar to a rapid test for a cold, giving them a preliminary idea of their home’s condition before seeking help from a professional, a process that can often take several months. Separately, the center has also developed the Poseidon AI system designed to increase water allocation speed and efficiency in fighting fires, Chang said. The system is designed to deal with quakes or other contingencies that trigger secondary fires, and has been used to put out 3,000 blazes in Taipei since becoming operational there in February, the center said. articles.title: Federal Web Architecture Re-Engineered to Accommodate Autonomous AI Scrapers
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Kaitlyn Levinson , Reporter, Route Fifty | October 19, 2026 As residents’ use of AI to find government information grows, a new report from the Beeck Center offers recommendations for officials to ensure their content doesn’t get excluded from outputs. Accessibility Artificial Intelligence Artificial intelligence is altering how constituents interact with their governments and services, as the technology is increasingly woven into benefits administration, public transportation and, now, website navigation, according to a new report. This presents an opportunity for governments to revise their public websites to ensure they remain a relevant source among artificial intelligence-enabled searches. “As more residents turn to AI assistants instead of visiting a government website directly, their ability to find the right answer increasingly depends on if that assistant can actually reach — and correctly interpret — government content,” a new report released last week from Georgetown University’s Beeck Center for Social Impact and Innovation reads. The report aims to help government staff responsible for technical and content decisions regarding government websites — such as IT offices, chief information officers or web design teams — prepare their content to be accessible for AI tools used to identify and relay such information, according to the report. State and local governments must automate digital accessibility processes Website accessibility remains ‘slow-moving crisis’ despite rule delay, experts warn Those tools are known as AI crawlers, or automated programs varying in scope and purpose that sweep websites to collect information, which are increasingly requiring agencies to consider how they design website access, structure and content accuracy, Andrew Merluzzi, artificial intelligence and incubation fellow at Georgetown University’s Beeck Center and report author, told Route Fifty . Generally, this “is not a super difficult thing for governments to fix, but they have to know they have this problem in the first place in order to go fix it,” he said, adding that “the main goal of this [report] was to try to help governments make the information transparent that they're already trying to make transparent.” One step government can take to improve AI crawler access is to assess their current website security configurations. Many websites include settings that block “malicious” bots, which could “inadvertently block a legitimate AI assistant trying to answer a person’s question,” the guidance reads. However, agencies must also balance AI crawler access with its potential impact on a website’s hosting capacity, due to increased traffic, according to the report. Government can consider a three-tier system to help determine how they approach granting access to certain AI crawlers through their website settings, such as a robots.txt file, Merluzzi said. The first tier of AI crawlers refers to tools from “established AI providers,” which the report recommends that a government allow to access its website when their identities can be verified. Such crawlers or crawler setting controls include OpenAI’s GPTbot, Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Googlebot, among others. In fact, “you don’t have to care about every possible [large language model] on the planet accessing your website — what you need to care about are the major tools that people are using every single day,” Merluzzi said. AI tools under the second tier may be developed from established providers but could have “narrower relevance” for resident use or have documented compliance concerns, according to the report. Before governments design their websites to allow such AI crawlers, staff can monitor and evaluate specific tools on a case-by-case basis. For bots that do not match a verified bot signature, which fall under the report’s third tier, government can implement a graduated response system of website access. For instance, staff can configure websites with unique responses to different bots, such as logging a potential bot that appears low risk for further review or automatically blocking traffic from a source highly likely to be a bot, Merluzzi explained. The report also points to website structure as a tool for building access for AI crawlers. Governments are spending considerable resources and time to improve the usability and interactivity of their websites with features like drop-down menus and clickable dashboards, but plainness and simplicity could be key with AI crawlers, Merluzzi said. “The implication here now for AI is just [to] publish a lot of that information as plain text, and that’s all you need to do so that the LLMs can then find a webpage … and read it and relay it back to the user who’s asking a question,” he said. In addition to more interactive webpages, government staff can publish critical information — such as deadlines for benefit program applications — as web page text, HTML tables or PDFs with extractable text and data, according to the report. Otherwise, scanned documents or screenshots containing relevant data for users may be overlooked by AI crawlers. Staff should also retest a website’s interaction with AI crawlers following major website redesigns or backend changes to a content management system, as such alterations “can affect whether AI crawlers and retrieval systems can access important information, even when the visible content appears unchanged,” according to the report. The accuracy of information on a website is another critical pillar to AI crawler preparation, Merluzzi said. Government should designate a specific person or team, separate from managing the website’s security against AI crawlers, to focus on content accuracy and timeliness, according to the report. These individuals can own the process for updating and correcting information across government websites, prioritizing data “consequence” rather than “volume,” the report reads. “A rarely-viewed page with a wrong emergency number matters more than a frequently-viewed page with a minor outdated statistic,” according to the report, which also recommends testing if an AI assistant pulls the correct and updated website data when queried. Unlike other “technology problems in state and local governments for which the solutions are not easy [because] they’re bureaucratic or likely to take many years,” Merluzzi said, reconfiguring websites to be more searchable by AI crawlers “is one where if you put a few people on this problem for a week or two, you could make really substantial progress without a ton of expertise.” Share This:
